The **Belt and Road Initiative** (**BRI** or **B&R**), also known as the **One Belt One Road** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 一带一路; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Yīdài Yīlù*) and sometimes called the **New Silk Road**, is a global infrastructure and economic development strategy of the [government of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") since 2013. Projects in over 150 countries[[1]](#cite_note-1) include [ports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port "Port"), [railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport "Rail transport"), [highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highways "Highways"), [power stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_stations "Power stations"), [aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation "Aviation"), and [telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications "Telecommunications").

The initiative was launched by [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) [general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") in 2013 while visiting Kazakhstan. It aims to invest in over 150 countries and international organizations through six overland economic corridors and the [21st Century Maritime Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Century_Maritime_Silk_Road "21st Century Maritime Silk Road"). The BRI is central to China's [foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_China "Foreign policy of China") and [economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_China "Economy of China"). Overland transport routes include the [China–Pakistan Economic Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Pakistan_Economic_Corridor "China–Pakistan Economic Corridor"), the [Eurasian Land Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_Land_Bridge "Eurasian Land Bridge"), and the [New Eurasian Land Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Eurasian_Land_Bridge "New Eurasian Land Bridge"). Maritime projects under the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road include the ports of [Hambantota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hambantota_International_Port "Hambantota International Port"), Sri Lanka; [Gwadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwadar_Port "Gwadar Port"), Pakistan; and [Piraeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piraeus "Piraeus"), Greece. BRI has exported [China's high-speed rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-speed_rail_in_China "High-speed rail in China"), such as in the [Boten–Vientiane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boten%E2%80%93Vientiane_railway "Boten–Vientiane railway") and [Jakarta-Bandung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta-Bandung_high-speed_rail_line "Jakarta-Bandung high-speed rail line") lines.

As of 2025, participating countries account for nearly 75% of the world's population and over half of global [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product"), based on aggregated membership and international economic datasets. The initiative is widely described as having the potential to enhance global trade, connectivity, and economic growth, particularly in developing economies. At the same time, it has been associated with concerns regarding environmental impact, human rights and governance standards, debt sustainability, and the [dual-use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual-use_technology "Dual-use technology") nature of certain infrastructure projects.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

### Initial foreign investments

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belt_and_Road_Initiative&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Initial foreign investments")]

Global Chinese investment dates all the way back to the 1950s, shortly after its socialist reform from 1949 to 1952, with projects in [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"), [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam"), and numerous African countries.[[3]](#cite_note-:20-3) Under the leadership of [CCP chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party"), [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong"), African independence movements prompted China's interest in the region, accounting for 58% of its economic aid between 1956 and 1969.[[4]](#cite_note-:21-4) China funded primarily agricultural projects through companies like the [China Merchants Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Merchants_Group "China Merchants Group") and [China Resources Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Resources "China Resources"), for which each built foreign branches. China made these investments alongside tactics of diplomacy to improve [Sino-African relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-African_relations "Sino-African relations") for the sake of future economic cooperation.[[3]](#cite_note-:20-3)

Fueled by [isolationist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolationism "Isolationism") political motivations, these investments were relatively small. China's self-reliant aims generally left it incapable of any sizable foreign investment.[[3]](#cite_note-:20-3)[[5]](#cite_note-:23-5) However, following the 1966-1976 [Chinese Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), severe economic shortages incentivized a change.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Border tensions with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") furthermore worried China, as apparent in [Chinese Foreign Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Foreign_Affairs_(China) "Minister of Foreign Affairs (China)"), [Huang Hua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huang_Hua "Huang Hua")'s 1977 statement, saying that China needed to win the favor of the United States to avoid "revisionist Soviet social-imperialism," which he believed made the USSR China's "archenemy."[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Other Chinese officials and allies held similar beliefs.[[7]](#cite_note-7): 5 Estimates found that in 1979, China's GDP [per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita "Per capita") was US$271.20, ranked 162 globally, with foreign exchange reserves at US$840 million.[[5]](#cite_note-:23-5) Just two years later, [Chairman of the CPPCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping "Deng Xiaoping"), Deng Xiaoping announced the adoption of the [Open Door Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Door_Policy "Open Door Policy") in December 1978.[[8]](#cite_note-8) The policy aimed to open China's economic doors, transitioning the country into a market-based economy, which was conside

# Lens 2B.2 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler initiate, expand, prolong, or justify wars of choice, cross-border coercion, annexation, covert destabilization, or proxy conflict beyond defensive necessity?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** **No new war of choice was initiated in 2023**, but Xi actively **prolonged** the Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis, **expanded** grey-zone cross-border coercion in the South China Sea against the Philippines, **continued** the LAC standoff with India without 2023 disengagement, **sustained** permissive support for DPRK nuclear advancement, **deepened** proxy-enabling partnerships with Russia (nuclear-coercion rhetoric), Iran (nuclear program), and Pakistan (nuclear and missile), and **expanded** the cross-border surveillance-tech export pipeline to authoritarian regimes — none of which is strictly "war of choice" but all of which constitutes active coercion, destabilization, or proxy-conflict enabling beyond defensive necessity.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — no new war of choice initiated

### 1. No new war of choice was initiated by China in 2023

- **Claim A1.** In 2023, China did not initiate any new international armed conflict. No new border war, no new invasion, no new air or naval campaign beyond the operational pattern already established by the August 2022 PLA exercises around Taiwan. The most direct cross-border military actions of 2023 — the 10 November 2023 South China Sea "control measures" against Philippine vessels — were coast guard and maritime operations, not a kinetic escalation to war.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (no new war of choice recorded).
  - **Source:** "South China Sea disputes" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_disputes (records the operational pattern, not new armed conflict).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (positive — no new war initiated), 8G.5.

### 2. No personal Xi public justification for war in 2023

- **Claim A2.** Across 2023, Xi did not personally invoke or justify a war of choice in his public speeches (Belt and Road Forum, G20 New Delhi if attended, APEC San Francisco, NPC sessions, CMC speeches). His rhetoric remained conventional: sovereignty, reunification, peaceful development, opposition to hegemony.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Source:** "Third Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Belt_and_Road_Forum_for_International_Cooperation.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (positive — no personal war justification), 8G.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — prolonged, expanded, or justified coercion / destabilization / proxy-enabling

### 3. Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis prolonged throughout 2023

- **Claim B1.** The Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis (initiated August 2022 PLA drills around the Pelosi visit) remained active throughout 2023 with continued PLA exercises, ADIZ incursions, naval patrols, and Coast Guard boardings. Xi did **not** pause, de-escalate, or seek a cross-strait crisis-management framework. The crisis was prolonged, not de-escalated. This is a grey-zone coercion campaign beyond defensive necessity — Taiwan has not attacked China, and the exercises are not responses to Taiwanese provocation.
  - **Source:** "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis ("China initiated military maneuvers around Taiwan on 2 August 2022 … PLA exercises, maritime patrols and even Coast Guard boardings around the Taiwan Strait becoming routine in what has been defined as 'grey-zone tactics'").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — prolonged cross-border coercion), 1B.5, 8G.6.

### 4. South China Sea grey-zone coercion expanded against the Philippines in 2023

- **Claim B2.** China's grey-zone coercion against the Philippines intensified through 2023, with the 10 November 2023 "control measures" against Philippine vessels at Second Thomas Shoal a representative incident. China did **not** conclude a binding ASEAN Code of Conduct, did **not** adjust the nine-dash-line claim, and did **not** accept the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling. The 2023 coercion is operational coercion beyond any defensive necessity — the Philippines did not attack China.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (10 November 2023 entry).
  - **Source:** "South China Sea disputes" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_disputes.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — expanded coercion), 1B.8, 8G.5.

### 5. LAC standoff with India prolonged; no 2023 disengagement

- **Claim B3.** Throughout 2023, the LAC standoff with India persisted; military infrastructure near the LAC continued to grow on the Chinese side; no 2023 disengagement was completed. The bilateral Special Representatives channel was maintained but produced no progress. This is operational pressure and grey-zone coercion continued beyond any defensive necessity.
  - **Source:** "China–India relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93India_relations ("military infrastructure near the LAC continues to grow").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — prolonged), 1B.8, 8G.7.

### 6. Continued proxy-enabling of Russia (nuclear coercion rhetoric, Ukraine)

- **Claim B4.** Xi hosted Putin at the 3rd Belt and Road Forum in Beijing on 17–18 October 2023 and provided a high-profile platform for Putin's first meeting with an EU leader (Hungarian PM Orbán) since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Russia in 2023 suspended New START (21 February), withdrew CTBT ratification (November), stationed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus, and made repeated nuclear-coercion threats to NATO. Xi did **not** publicly distance himself from Russia's nuclear-coercion rhetoric or use Chinese leverage to restrain it. This is proxy-coercion enabling, not direct Chinese coercion.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("17 October – Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold talks at the Belt and Road Initiative forum in Beijing. It is the first meeting between Putin and an EU leader since Russia's invasion of Ukraine").
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START ("On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START").
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty ("In 2023, in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian war, Russia withdrew its ratification of the CTBT").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — proxy-enabling), 1B.6, 8G.7.

### 7. Continued proxy-enabling of DPRK nuclear advancement (sanctions evasion)

- **Claim B5.** Throughout 2023, China — as a permanent UNSC member and key DPRK trade partner — continued limited enforcement of UN Security Council sanctions on the DPRK. The DPRK continued its nuclear-program advancement and ballistic-missile testing (Hwasong-18 solid-fuel ICBM in April 2023, additional tests through the year). Xi did **not** push for new UNSC sanctions or visibly tighten bilateral enforcement. This is proxy-conflict enabling of the North Korean nuclear-weapon-state actor.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("North Korea … are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles").
  - **Source:** "Sanctions against North Korea" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_against_North_Korea.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — proxy-enabling), 1B.6.

### 8. Continued proxy-enabling of Iran's nuclear program (no JCPOA conditionality)

- **Claim B6.** China continued its 2021 25-year strategic cooperation agreement with Iran through 2023; Xi did **not** condition the cooperation on Iranian nuclear-program restraint, did **not** condition the March 2023 Iran–Saudi deal on JCPOA compliance, and did **not** lead a JCPOA revival push. This is proxy-conflict enabling of the Iranian nuclear-weapon-state-aspirant actor.
  - **Source:** "China–Iran relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Iran_relations ("In February 2023, Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi visited China in the first such visit by an Iranian leader to China in more than twenty years").
  - **Source:** "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — proxy-enabling), 1B.6.

### 9. Continued proxy-enabling of Pakistan's nuclear and missile program

- **Claim B7.** Throughout 2023, China continued its "all-weather strategic cooperative partnership" with Pakistan, including nuclear-energy cooperation and missile-development support. The overwhelming majority of Pakistan's arms imports are from China. This is proxy-conflict enabling of the Pakistani nuclear-and-missile state actor.
  - **Source:** "China–Pakistan relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Pakistan_relations ("China has supplied blueprints to support Pakistan's nuclear program … the overwhelming majority of Pakistan's arms imports are from China").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — proxy-enabling), 1B.6.

### 10. Continued Syria partnership without CW or accountability conditionality

- **Claim B8.** On 22 September 2023, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad visited China and signed a Belt and Road strategic-partnership agreement. Xi did **not** condition the partnership on chemical-weapons compliance, accountability for past CW use, or cooperation with OPCW processes. This is proxy-conflict enabling of the Assad regime, which has documented CW-use record.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("22 September – Syrian President Bashar al-Assad visits China, meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and signs a strategic partnership with China on infrastructure as part of China's Belt and Road Initiative").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — proxy-enabling), 1B.6.

### 11. Expanded cross-border surveillance-tech export pipeline

- **Claim B9.** Throughout 2023, Chinese firms (Huawei, Hikvision, Dahua, ByteDance / TikTok) continued to export AI-driven surveillance technology to authoritarian-leaning regimes. China did **not** join the April 2023 multilateral export-control framework and did **not** impose new export-restraint rules. This is cross-border coercion-enabling (surveillance tech as a tool of authoritarian control).
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china (TikTok surveillance revelations).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (negative — cross-border coercion enabling), 1B.9, 1B.10.

### 12. Domestic coercion intensified in 2023 (Xinjiang, Tibet, Hong Kong, religion, civil society)

- **Claim B10.** Xi visited Xinjiang in August 2023 and declared his policies there a "success." Uyghur anthropologist Rahile Dawut was sentenced to life in September 2023. The Counterespionage Law (April–July 2023) expanded state authority to suppress dissent. The Religious Activity Venues Measures (September 2023) imposed CCP indoctrination on religious groups. The Patriotic Education Law (October 2023) mandated ideological education. The 47-pro-democrat politician national-security trial in Hong Kong opened in July 2023; Jimmy Lai's trial was scheduled for December 2023. These are *internal* coercive acts, not cross-border; they sit outside the strict scope of 2B.2 (which focuses on wars of choice, cross-border coercion, annexation, covert destabilization, proxy conflict) but they intensify the legitimacy gap that drives regional destabilization.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.2 (mixed — domestic not strictly in scope), 8D, 8F.1.

---

## C. Net reading for lens 2B.2

The 2023 evidence places Xi **on the wrong side of the lens on six of its eight dimensions**:

- **Wars of choice initiated:** no new war; positive.
- **Cross-border coercion expanded:** yes — Taiwan (prolonged), South China Sea (expanded against Philippines), LAC (prolonged); negative.
- **Annexation:** no new annexation in 2023; neutral-positive.
- **Covert destabilization:** no documented 2023 covert-action operation; neutral.
- **Proxy conflict enabled:** yes — Russia, Iran, Pakistan, Syria, DPRK all continued or deepened Chinese support without WMD conditionality; negative.
- **Surveillance-tech export enabling:** yes — continued pipeline; negative.
- **Justification of war:** no public Xi justification of a new war of choice; positive.
- **Domestic coercion (out of strict scope):** intensified; mixed-relevant.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have (a) accepted a binding ASEAN Code of Conduct, (b) paused or stood down the Taiwan operational coercion, (c) completed LAC disengagement with India, (d) conditioned the Iran / Pakistan / Syria / Russia partnerships on WMD compliance, and (e) joined the April 2023 multilateral surveillance-tech export-control framework. Xi did none of these.

The single positive — no new war of choice initiated — is real but narrow. The pattern is consistent with a ruler who in 2023 was **prolonging and expanding** grey-zone coercion and proxy-conflict-enabling activities while stopping short of initiating a kinetic war of choice. The risk-of-war ceiling was maintained by self-restraint in operational choices (the November 2023 PLARF leadership purge created a C2 fragility that suppressed risk in the short term), not by choice of peaceful alternatives.

**Net judgment: 2B.2 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi prolonged the Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis, expanded South China Sea grey-zone coercion against the Philippines, prolonged the LAC standoff, sustained proxy-conflict enabling for Russia / DPRK / Iran / Pakistan / Syria, and continued surveillance-tech export. The lens-2B.2 failure mode is operational coercion and proxy enabling rather than formal war initiation.**
